newsitem.title: USA: Gold back to 30-year average real price - Green.
newsitem.headline: Gold back to 30-year average real price - Green.

text.p: Despite long-term trends such as rising gold mine output and net central bank gold sales, gold may now be a bargain, said Timothy Green, gold industry consultant and author of the book "The World of Gold."

"In inflation-adjusted terms, gold is now not only cheaper than it was for the last 40 years of the 19th century, it is also back to its real average price of the last 130 years," Green told Gold and Silver Institute Conference here.

Outlining the major trends in the gold industry since gold prices were freed to trade at market rates in 1968, from the $35 an ounce imposed under the post-1945 Bretton Woods world monetary system, Green said gold had been through a mining revolution, a demand revolution, and a price revolution.
Until the early 1980's there were only two main gold producers -- South Africa and the Soviet Union.
But South Africa's share of production has fallen to around 22 percent of world output, while the U.S. has seen a 10-fold increase in mine output and Australia a 17-fold increase.

"On my own database I now have no less than 298 potential new mines in 53 countries," Green said. "The Gold Institute's most recent world gold production forecasts show an inexorable rise to the year 1999 and that's without counting the ubiqitous Bre-X in Indonesia where the motto seems to be, 'each week double the last number you thought of for reserves', but let's allow it probably is the biggest gold discovery of the 20th century."

The junior Canadian mining house Bre-X Minerals recently negotiated a deal with the Indonesian government and the large U.S. mining house, Freeport-McMoran Copper and Gold, to develop an estimated 71 million ounce reserve known as the Busang desposit, in Borneo, Indonesia.

"The essential factor to understand is the forces that have been let loose by that high gold price of the early 1980's (when gold reached $800 an ounce)," Green said. "We have a brand new gold mining industry that needs every year to find new reserves."
But also on the supply side, in the last 30 years, central banks have also turned into net sellers of gold, selling over 3,500 tonnes or 110 million ounces since 1965 on a net basis.
On the demand side, no-one would have foreseen that fabrication demand in jewelry and industry would easily exceed new gold mine production every year by the 1990's, he said.

"Until the 1960s, the ready-made buyers were largely governments or central banks," Green said. "A gold mining boom in the 1930's was underwritten by the U.S. Treasury standing ready to buy all gold offered to it at the then new high price of $35 an ounce."

He said, "Even between 1948 and 1964, 44 percent of all newly mined gold was taken up by central banks, but since then they have become net sellers and they will continue to be, but not in excessive amounts. The large amounts of gold in European central bank vaults may be mainly sterilized by putting some towards backing for the new Euro currency due probably in 1999. But the gold miner's client now is the jewelry buyer and the industrial user to a lesser extent."

He added, "Just as photography came along at the beginning of this century to give silver a real demand base, so gold now has a real demand base in jewelry. The mystery man in the gold industry is the investor."
The ordinary investor bought close to 300 tonnes (almost 10 million ounces) annually of bullion coins in the best years of the 1970's, but last year it was only 65 tonnes (two million ounces).
"A switch into gold now actually means gold shares," Green said. "The action is in the shares, not the metal itself and in my view that is a real problem for gold as a metal."
